Please find below *Employment law research for Mexico:*

*Employment law research for Mexico:*

 *1. Is the market subject to laws where an employment relationship can be deemed or implied?*

Yes. Pursuant to the Mexican Federal Labor Law (“+FLL+”), an employment relationship exists, irrespective of the act of origin, whenever the following elements are met (i) provision of personal service; (ii) the individual providing the service is subordinated to the beneficiary and; (iii) the service is compensated by the payment of a salary. Since the existence of employment agreements is a fact (or omission) attributable to employers, an employment relationship may be determined by the relevant authorities even if no employment agreement was executed, by the existence of the beforementioned elements.

 *2.* *Is there any evidence that platforms are under scrutiny under the legal system (litigation etc.)?*

Yes. The nature of the relationship between the platforms and the partners/riders/operators (gig workers) and the possibility of modifying the applicable regulation has been in the political agenda from a couple of years and there are still potential amendments being discussed in the Mexican congress. Irrespective of the foregoing, in our experience it is still a functional and fairly common arrangement on specific industries.

 *3. Is the relevant test subject to express presumption criteria?*

Please note that pursuant to the FLL there are no applicable tests pursuant to determining whether an individual should be deemed as a contractor or an employee as they have in the US (IRS or common law test). To the extent that a relationship has the elements described in our first response, the risk of such being determined as an employment arrangement is increased (materiality would depend on a potential claim).

 *4.* *Are reclassification-sensitive activities expressly considered by a court or any law to imply an employment relationship?*

Yes, elements of subordination within the relationship in terms of which there is a mandate to obey and the subsequent right to order from the company, would be generally considered as trigger for determining the existence of an employment relationship. A similar argument may exist if the individual is subject to a specific work schedule or if its given work-related tools.

 *5. Can claims be made in respect of past periods (i.e. for previously withheld earnings)?*

There is a statute of limitation of one year for employees to claim the observance of employment obligations (i.e., payment of benefits). Therefore, if and when an employment relationship was to be determined by the relevant authorities with the platform, the employees would only be entitled to claim payment for benefits for the previous year. Likewise, the contractors have a two-month statute of limitation in order to claim the misclassification of their relationship (if terminated).

 *6.* *Who is able to take action against Bolt? Drivers / group action / regulators?*

Correct, the drivers would be able to claim the misclassification of the relationship in order to seek protection from employment laws in Mexico. Furthermore, the relevant tax, social security and employment authorities could potentially inspect Bolt’s compliance with its employer obligations – if an employment relationship was to be determined. Lastly, unions could potentially pursuit action against Bolt arguing the representation of the contractors as employees.

 *7. Is there any evidence that the authorities have considered Drivers eligible for employment benefits in the past (e.g. tax authorities, pension authorities, etc)?*

We understand that there are individual cases in which the employment authorities have effectively considered drivers as employees pursuant to the FLL – however, these resolutions are not collectively binding and there is no public information on the particulars of the cases and on whether or not the determinations in a first instance were challenged by the companies.

 *8.* *What is the level of access to justice in a market (e.g. high state duties, the requirement to have a representative, etc.)?*

While it is not necessary to have a legal representative in order to access the justice system, it is extremely common to undertake such an alternative. As a general remark, the Mexican employment culture tends to be more inclined towards litigation than others as the FLL and the employment justice system is more prone to benefit employees, rather than employers.

 *9. Can claims be made to reclassify all Drivers of the platform in a market at once?*

The misclassification claims would have to be filed individually by the relevant contractors; the materiality of the claims would depend on the elements they would have in each case for the purpose of demonstrating that the relationship was that of an employment nature (depending on the existence of the elements described in the first question) – the potential resolutions would have no binding effects one from the other. The foregoing in the understanding that if an amendment to the FLL is approved in terms of which it sets forth the obligation for gig personnel to be considered as employees, such would have a general or market-wide effect.

*_Feedback from our OC_*

The only thing to flag is that, until such time as the 14 day period has expired – you will arguably have no enforceable contracts in place with any partners, even the ones that have properly filled out the form, because there is no certainty of contract from their side. So to have wording stating that “there is a contract unless Bolt determines in its sole discretion that there isn’t” doesn’t, in my view, work.Also, you may end up in a situation where the email is missed, and a partner can claim that they thought there was a valid contract when, in fact, there wasn’t.The bottom line is that the below approach opens you up to uncertainty and [dispute.My|http://dispute.My] view is that partners should fill out the form first – once Bolt is satisfied that the form has been properly filled in, the partners should get a notification asking them to accept the general terms, which then stipulates that, upon such acceptance, there is a valid contract in [place.|http://place.An]

[An|http://place.An] alternative approach would be that Bolt will confirm to the Partner within 14 days that the Agreement is binding:*_Upon acceptance of the General Terms by the Partner and submission of this form to Bolt, the Agreement shall become legally binding on receipt of a notice from Bolt that it has accepted the form submitted by the Partner, in its own sole discretion. Should such confirmation not be provided within 14 days of submitting the form, the form shall be deemed rejected and no Agreement will come into force._*

As far as I understand it, Fleet Operators are not considered employees of Bolt, however the relevant act here defines an employee as:

{{"employee" means any person who has entered into or works under a contract of service, or any person who has undertaken personally to execute any work or service for, and under the immediate direction and control of another person, including an outworker, but excluding work or service performed in a professional capacity or as a contractor for another person when such work or service is not regulated by a specific contract of service;}}

If we decide Fleet Operators should be considered employees under this definition, we have a sufficient legal basis. If we decide they are not considered employees, then we do not.

Hello! 

The aim of the verification procedure is to ensure us the user is a legitimate one and to alleviate the potential of them defrauding Bolt. Essentially, this should be prompted if we detect irregular activities or the risk of the user being problematic. This risk profiling includes the possibilities of users potentially having payment issues (not paying for their services) and not just actively engaging in fraud schemes - there are a lot of things contributing to the user’s risk score/fraud score. 

In general, not only do we have direct indications such as we know that certain domains are bad or certain cards are suspicious, but we also look at business users as a group and what are the most common issues in this group. So, if we can see a certain problematic thing has a constant payment issue or high fraud rate then we adjust any users in this group to being risky. A lot of the time the users will not see or feel our risk profiling as they have not reached the thresholds of what we consider a ‘breaking point’ or ‘significant risk’, however, if things have a very high or total rate of failure, we start being more aggressive as there is also a very high likelihood of these users ending up being problematic and, as a default recovery option, verification helps us to be assured the user is good or at least we have a certain assurance on which we could rely on in case of illegal activities. 

While we understand that business admins and owners do not fully see the reasoning behind these actions, it is a way to protect us as well as ensure a seamless experience for users going forward. After verification, we trust the users and can offer non-frictional services as verification is kind of like whitelisting and counteracts the risk we see. 

You may assure the user that our verification services are completely protected - their data is safe and will not be used anywhere else. 

And I can see this user and business were profiled to have a higher risk than normal - so the way out would be successful verification or accumulated good history to counteract the risk we see.  

To locate the issues/get insight, you may check out the user’s calculations and our decisions: [https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fraud/userCalculationResults?filter={"limit"%3A25%2C"offset"%3A0%2C"filter"%3A{"user_id"%3A86459626%2C"from"%3A1681376036.606}}|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fraud/userCalculationResults?filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22user_id%22%3A86459626%2C%22from%22%3A1681376036.606%7D%7D]

* Currently vehicles in the categories “Bolt” and “XL” are eligible for the “Assist” category.

* The TVDE law establishes obligations in relation to passengers with reduced mobility (article 6).
* In particular, the law establishes that electronic platforms must provide a way to individuals with reduced mobility to have a ride on a vehicle capable of accommodating them and their wheelchair. 
* All the vehicles in the “XL” category can accommodate wheelchairs, but not all the vehicles in the “Bolt” category can. 
* Therefore, having only “XL” vehicles eligible for “Assist” category would therefore appear not to be against the TVDE law requirements.
* However, *we recommend that the following measures are further implement to ensure compliance with TVDE law*:
** Information in Bolt’s website (e.g. FAQ) is provided to clarify that the eligibility for “Assist” is only for “XL” vehicles in order to ensure that the rider always travels in a larger vehicle that is capable of transporting his/her means of locomotion (this is to ensure compliance with article 6.1);
** Information in Bolt’s website (e.g. FAQ) is provided to clarify to the rider that the price calculation for “Assist” is exactly the same as for the “XL” category (this is to ensure compliance with article 6.4)
